label: arch
text: One of the main components of Media Store is a server-side web front end, namely the Facade component, which delivers websites to the users and provides session management.

label: other
text: To meet the user authentication requirement, registration and log-in have to be offered.

label: arch
text: To this end, the Facade component delivers the corresponding registration and log-in pages to users.

label: other
text: After the user has logged into the system, he or she will be forwarded to a site to list the audio files.

label: other
text: The main functionality, however, is provided by other components.

label: arch
text: In addition, users can browse, download, and upload audio files using the Facade component.

label: arch
text: Application business logic is provided by a central business logic component, called the MediaManagement component.

label: arch
text: The MediaManagement component coordinates the communication of other components.

label: arch
text: Furthermore, it fetches audio files from a specific location (e.g., a dedicated file server or a local disk) when processing download requests.

label: other
text: As described above, to communicate with the system, users' registration and authentication are needed.

label: arch
text: The UserManagement component answers the requests for registration and authentication.

label: arch
text: The UserDBAdapter component queries the database.

label: arch
text: When a user logs into the system, Media Store does not store the password in plain text, but rather the UserManagement component implements further functions to hash and salt the passwords.

label: other
text: To reduce the risk of copyright infringements, all downloaded files are watermarked.

label: other
text: To this end, the requested files are first reencoded.

label: arch
text: The re-encoded files are then digitally and individually watermarked by the TagWatermarking component.

label: arch
text: Afterward, the MediaManagement component forwards these audio files from the TagWatermarking component to the user.

label: other
text: Hence, each downloaded audio file is uniquely connected to a user ID can can be associated with the user if the audio file should ever appear in the public Internet.

label: arch
text: To allow users to download several files at a time, we provide the Packaging component, which archives multiple audio files into a single compressed file.

label: arch
text: The ReEncoder component converts the bit rates of audio files.

label: other
text: This can result in reduction of file sizes.

label: other
text: The persistence tier contains components that are concerned with the storage of audio files and their meta-data.

label: arch
text: The Database component represents an actual database (e.g., MySQL).

label: arch
text: It stores user information and meta-data of audio files such as the name and the genre.

label: arch
text: After the user calls the page to list all available audio files, AudioAccess creates a query that is sent to the Database component.

label: arch
text: When a user uploads an audio file, the MediaAccess component stores it at the predefined location.

label: arch
text: The MediaAccess component encapsulates database access for meta-data of audio files.

label: arch
text: Furthermore, it fetches a list of all available audio files.

label: arch
text: By contrast, the UserDBAdapter component provides all functions required in order to encapsulate database access for the user data.

label: arch
text: The UserDBAdapter component creates a query based on the user's request.

label: arch
text: The Database component then executes the actual query for files.

label: arch
text: All salted hashes of passwords are also stored in the Database component.

label: arch
text: By contrast, all audio files are stored in a specific location (e.g., a dedicated file server or a local disk) to decouple the DataStorage from the database.

label: arch
text: When a user requests files to download, the MediaAccess component fetches the associated meta-data from the Database.

label: arch
text: Afterwards, based on the user request and the corresponding meta-data, the file will be retrieved from the DataStorage.

label: arch
text: When a user uploads a file, it will be stored in the DataStorage without any change.

label: other
text: However, a download can cause re-encoding of the audio file.

label: arch
text: The TeaStore consists of 5 replicatable services and a single Registry instance.

label: arch
text: The WebUI service retrieves images from the Image Provider.

label: arch
text: Users are authenticated by the Auth service.

label: arch
text: Data is retrieved from the PersistenceProvider and product recommendations from the Recommender service.

label: arch
text: The WebUI provides the TeaStore front-end using Servlets in combination with JSP files.

label: arch
text: It contains logic to save and retireve values from cookies.

label: arch
text: Images (with few exceptions) are not provides by the WebUi, but are retrieved from the Image Provider service instead.

label: arch
text: The UI provides a status page at link indicating the current state of the TeaStore.

label: impl
text: The status view lists the instance count and hosts for all registered service instances.

label: arch
text: The Image Provider delivers images to the WebUI as base64 encoded strings to embed them in the final HTML.

label: arch
text: It matches the provided product ID or UI name (the filename for images not representing a product and therefore without product ID) and the image size to a unique image identifier.

label: arch
text: If the product ID or UI name is not available to the Image Provider, a standard "not found" image will be delivered in the correct size.

label: impl
text: If the product ID or UI name is found but not in the requested size, the largest image will be loaded and scaled.

label: impl
text: The scaled image is stored for later use.

label: impl
text: If the product ID or UI name and size is found, the image will be loaded and delivered.

label: impl
text: To speed up image delivery, an in-memory cache with Least Frequently Used (LFU) replacemenent strategy is in place.

label: impl
text: Before loading an image from the physical drive, a cache lookup will be performed and if the image is present, delivered directly from cache or from the physical drive otherwise.

label: arch
text: The Auth service handles user and session authentication.

label: impl
text: Passwords are hashed using BCrypt.

label: impl
text: To validate sessions, the SessionBlob is salted and hashed using SHA512 and stored in a cookie.

label: impl
text: When a SessionBlob is received, the cookie content is re-salted and checked against the hash to check for session tampering.

label: arch
text: The Persistence service provides access to the data persisted in the relational database back-end.

label: impl
text: It maps the relational entities to the JSON entity objects passed between services using the EclipseLink JPA ORM mapper.

label: arch
text: It features endpoints for general CRUD-Operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) for the persistent entities.

label: impl
text: The persistence provider uses a second level entity cache provided by the JPA implementation.

label: arch
text: As such, it also acts as a caching layer.

label: arch
text: The Recommender is used to generate individual product recommendations for each user.

label: arch
text: It is trained using all existing orders.

label: impl
text: Recommendations are generated based on the users current shopping cart, the user's previous orders and/or the item the user is currently looking at.

label: impl
text: The item rating of the users are based on their purchases.

label: impl
text: If the current user is unknown (e.g., if the user is not logged in or did not purchase anything yet), a fallback algorithm based on the general item popularity is chosen.

label: impl
text: If the user is known, Slope One as item-based collaborative filtering is applied to calculate the recommendations.

label: impl
text: We implemented two versions of the algorithm.

label: impl
text: One CPU-intensive, calculating the item-rankings per user on-the-go and one memory-intensive, calculating the total user rating prediction matrix during the training phase.

label: impl
text: Furthermore, one order-based nearest-neighbor approach is available.

label: impl
text: Its recommendation time is dependent on the number of items in the current cart as well as the total number of stored orders.

label: arch
text: The Registry provides information about how many service instances are online for each service and where they are located.

label: arch
text: Service instances register themselves at the registry on startup.

label: impl
text: Services are also required to send a heartbeat signal by re-registering periodically.

label: impl
text: Services missing their heartbeat for more than 10 s are assumed to be offline until the register function is called again.

label: impl
text: Every running instance of the TeaStore uses one single registry.

label: other
text: The TeaStore is a test application.

label: impl
text: By limiting it to a single registry instance, it enables easy configuration of multiple parallel TeaStores with minimal configuration overhead.

label: arch
text: The UI component is the first stop for 99% of all requests that are received by the application.

label: meta
text: Such a request will go through the following steps.

label: impl
text: First, request received by the GAE server.

label: impl
text: Second, custom filters are applied according to the order specified in web.xml, e.g. OriginCheckFilter.

label: impl
text: Third, request forwarded to a Servlet object as specified in web.xml for further processing, depending on the type of request.

label: other
text: There are two general types of requests.

label: other
text: The user-invoked requests and the automated (GAE server-invoked) requests, which are processed differently.

label: other
text: User-invoked requests are all requests made by the users of the application, typically from the Web browser (i.e. by navigating to a particular URL of the application).

label: meta
text: The request will be processed as in the image.

label: meta
text: The initial request for the web page will be processed as follows.

label: impl
text: First, request forwarded to WebPageServlet.

label: impl
text: Second, WebPageServlet returns the built single web page (index.html).

label: impl
text: Third, the browser will render the page and execute the page scripts, most of the time requiring AJAX requests to the server.

label: meta
text: Subsequent AJAX requests sent to the server will be processed as follows.

label: impl
text: First, request forwarded to the WebApiServlet.

label: impl
text: Second, WebApiServlet uses the ActionFactory to generate the matching Action object, e.g. InstructorHomePageAction.

label: impl
text: Third, WebApiServlet executes the action.

label: impl
text: Fourth, the Action object checks the access rights of the user.

label: arch
text: If the action is allowed, it will be performed, interacting with the Logic component as necessary.

label: impl
text: Fifth, the Action packages and processes the result into an ActionResult object.

label: impl
text: The most common format is JsonResult (requests for obtaining data or processing existing data), and other formats are defined as necessary, e.g. FileDownloadResult (e.g. downloading feedback session report) and ImageResult (e.g. profile pictures).

label: impl
text: Sixth, WebApiServlet sends the result back to the browser which will then process it on the front-end.

label: impl
text: Requests for static asset files (e.g. CSS, JS files, images) are served directly without going through web.xml configuration at all.

label: impl
text: The Web API is protected by two layers of access control check.

label: impl
text: These are origin check, authentication and authorization check.

label: impl
text: Origin check mitigates CSRF attack.

label: impl
text: Authentication and authorization check checks if the logged in user (or lack thereof) has sufficient privileges to trigger the API's actions.

label: impl
text: Special keys (csrf key and backdoor key) can be used to bypass each of the checks, typically for testing purpose.

label: impl
text: Those keys are strings known only to the person who deployed the application (typically, the administrator).

label: impl
text: Automated requests are all requests sent automatically by the GAE server during specific periods of time.

label: meta
text: This type of request will be processed as follows.

label: impl
text: First, the source of the request will be checked for administrator privilege.

label: impl
text: If this privilege is absent (e.g. non-administrator users trying to invoke the automated actions), the request will be dropped and a 403 Forbidden status will be returned.

label: impl
text: Second, requests generated by the GAE server are equipped with this privilege.

label: impl
text: Third, administrators can manually invoke these requests.

label: impl
text: This is particularly useful in testing the actions associated with those requests.

label: impl
text: Fourth, request forwarded to the AutomatedServlet.

label: impl
text: Fifth, automatedServlet uses the AutomatedActionFactory to generate the matching AutomatedAction object, e.g. CompileLogsAction.

label: impl
text: Sixth, automatedServlet executes the action.

label: arch
text: Seventh, the corresponding AutomatedAction will be performed, interacting with the Logic component as necessary.

label: impl
text: GAE server sends such automated requests through two different configurations.

label: impl
text: These configurations are cron jobs or task queue workers.

label: impl
text: Cron jobs are jobs that are automatically scheduled for a specified period of time, e.g. scheduling feedback session opening reminders.

label: impl
text: It is configured in cron.xml.

label: impl
text: Task queue workers are hybrids of user-invoked and GAE-invoked in that they are queued by users (i.e. users request for the tasks to be added to queue), but executed by GAE (i.e. GAE determines when and which tasks in the queue are executed at any point of time).

label: impl
text: This is typically used for tasks that may take a long time to finish and can exceed the 1 minute standard request processing limit imposed by GAE.

label: impl
text: It is configured in queue.xml as well as the TaskQueue nested class of the Const class.

label: impl
text: Since the high-level workflow of processing a request is same for any request (differing by the two request types only), we use the Template Method pattern to abstract the process flow into the Action and AutomatedAction classes.

label: arch

label: impl

label: arch
text: Eventual consistency here means it takes some time for a database operation to propagate across all serves of the Google's distributed datastore.

label: arch
text: We have been successfully transitioning from a spaghetti to a more structured architecture with the model in the center, and the logic as an intermediate layer towards the gui which is the outer shell.

label: arch
text: There are additional utility packages for preferences and the cli.

label: arch
text: The dependencies are only directed towards the center.

label: impl
text: We have JUnit tests to detect violations of the most crucial dependencies (between logic, model, and gui), and the build will fail automatically in these cases.

label: arch
text: The model represents the most important data structures (BibDatases, BibEntries, Events, and related aspects) and has only a little bit of logic attached.

label: arch
text: The logic is responsible for reading/writing/importing/exporting and manipulating the model, and it is structured often as an API the gui can call and use.

label: arch
text: Only the gui knows the user and his preferences and can interact with him to help him solve tasks.

label: arch
text: For each layer, we form packages according to their responsibility, i.e., vertical structuring.

label: arch
text: The model should have no dependencies to other classes of JabRef and the logic should only depend on model classes.

label: arch
text: The cli package bundles classes that are responsible for JabRef’s command line interface.

label: arch
text: The preferences represents all information customizable by a user for her personal needs.

label: arch
text: We use an event bus to publish events from the model to the other layers.

label: arch
text: This allows us to keep the architecture but still react upon changes within the core in the outer layers.

text: The HTML5 server is built upon Meteor.js in ECMA2015 for communication between client and server and upon MongoDB for keeping the state of each BigBlueButton client consistent with the BigBlueButton server.

label: arch
text: The MongoDB database contains information about all meetings on the server and, in turn, each client connected to a meeting.

label: arch
text: Each user's client is only aware of the their meeting's state, such the user's public and private chat messages sent and received.

label: arch
text: The client side subscribes to the published collections on the server side.

label: arch
text: Updates to MongoDB on the server side are automatically pushed to MiniMongo on the client side.

label: meta
text: Scalability of HTML5 server component.

label: impl
text: BigBlueButton 2.2 used a single nodejs process for all client-side communication.

label: impl
text: This process would start to bottleneck (the nodejs process, running on a single CPU core, started to use 100% of the core).

label: impl
text: Because nodejs was running on a single CPU core, having a 16 or 32 CPU core server for BigBlueButton 2.2 failed to yield much additional scalability.

label: arch
text: BigBlueButton 2.3 moves away from a single nodejs process for bbb-html5 towards multiple nodejs processes handling incoming messages from clients.

label: arch
text: This means that bbb-html5 could use multiple CPU cores for processing messages and handling browser sessions (each nodejs process runs on a single CPU core).

label: impl
text: As of 2.3-alpha-7, bbb-html5 uses 2 "frontend" and two "backend" processes (this value is configurable in bbb-html5-with-roles.conf, see Configuration Files).

label: impl
text: A restart of BigBlueButton is required if you make changes to these files.

label: meta
text: The breakdown of functionality between front-end and back-end is as follows.

label: impl
text: Frontends receive the ValidateAuthTokenResp event to complete authentication.

label: impl
text: Frontends collect subscriptions and publishers.

label: impl
text: Frontends receive other DDP events including method calls to send events to akka-apps.

label: impl
text: Frontends handle completely the Streamer redis events, i.e., Cursor, Annotations, External video share.

label: impl
text: Frontends still require MeetingStarted and MeetingEnded events to create/destroy per-meeting event processing queues.

label: impl
text: Backends handle all the non-streamer events.

label: arch
text: If more than one backend is running, bbb-web splits the load in round-robin fashion by assigning an instanceId.

label: impl
text: So individual backends only process redis events for the meetings matching the associated instanceId.

label: impl
text: ValidateAuthTokenResp is passed to backends as well, which is needed for the cases where you only have a backend, no frontends - for example dev environments that do not need to care about scaling.

label: impl
text: When you use sudo bbb-conf --setip <hostname> or sudo bbb-conf --restart, bbb-conf will run /etc/bigbluebutton/bbb-conf/apply-config.sh between shutdown and restart of the BigBlueButton processes.

label: impl
text: In this way, you can change configuration values of BigBlueButton, or use some of the helper functions in apply-lib.sh.

label: meta
text: See "Automatically apply configuration changes on restart".

text: BBB web.

label: arch
text: BigBlueButton web application is a Java-based application written in Scala.

label: arch
text: It implements the BigBlueButton API and holds a copy of the meeting state.

label: arch
text: The BigBlueButton API provides a third-party integration (such as the BigBlueButtonBN plugin for Moodle) with an endpoint to control the BigBlueButton server.

label: other
text: Every access to BigBlueButton comes through a front-end portal (we refer to as a third-party application).

label: other
text: BigBlueButton integrates Moodle, Wordpress, Canvas, Sakai, and others (see third-party integrations).

label: other
text: BigBlueButton comes with its own front-end called Greenlight.

label: other
text: When using a learning management system (LMS) such as Moodle, teachers can setup BigBlueButton rooms within their course and students can access the rooms and their recordings.

label: other
text: The BigBlueButton comes with some simple API demos.

label: other
text: Regardless of which front-end you use, they all use the API under the hood.

text: Redis PubSub.

label: arch
text: Redis PubSub provides a communication channel between different applications running on the BigBlueButton server.

label: meta
text: Redis DB.

label: arch
text: When a meeting is recorded, all events are stored in Redis DB.

label: arch
text: When the meeting ends, the Recording Processor will take all the recorded events as well as the different raw (PDF, WAV, FLV) files for processing.

label: arch
text: BigBlueButton Apps is the main application that pulls together the different applications to provide real-time collaboration in the meeting.

label: arch
text: It provides the list of users, chat, whiteboard, presentations in a meeting.

text: FSESL akka.

label: arch
text: We have extracted out the component that integrates with FreeSWITCH into it’s own application.

label: arch
text: This allows others who are using voice conference systems other than FreeSWITCH to easily create their own integration.

label: arch
text: Communication between apps and FreeSWITCH Event Socket Layer (fsels) uses messages through redis pubsub.

label: meta
text: FreeSWITCH.

label: other
text: We think FreeSWITCH is an amazing piece of software for handling audio.

label: arch
text: FreeSWITCH provides the voice conferencing capability in BigBlueButton.

label: arch
text: Users are able to join the voice conference through the headset.

label: arch
text: Users joining through Google Chrome or Mozilla Firefox are able to take advantage of higher quality audio by connecting using WebRTC.

label: arch
text: FreeSWITCH can also be integrated with VOIP providers so that users who are not able to join using the headset will be able to call in using their phone.

label: meta
text: Kurento and WebRTC-SFU.

label: arch
text: Kurento Media Server KMS is a media server that implements both SFU and MCU models.

label: arch
text: KMS is responsible for streaming of webcams, listen-only audio, and screensharing.

label: arch
text: The WebRTC-SFU acts as the media controller handling negotiations and to manage the media streams.

label: meta
text: Joining a voice conference.

label: arch
text: A user can join the voice conference (running in FreeSWITCH) from the BigBlueButton HTML5 client or through the phone.

label: arch
text: When joining through the client, the user can choose to join Microphone or Listen Only, and the BigBlueButton client will make an audio connection to the server via WebRTC.

label: other
text: WebRTC provides the user with high-quality audio with lower delay.

label: arch

label: arch
text: The conversion process sends progress messages to the client through the Redis pubsub.
